one_line: Better Stack explains the Ralph loop (a bash while-loop that reruns one prompt with a fresh context each time) and why the official Claude Code Ralph plugin, with compaction and iteration caps, drifts from the canonical design.
summary: The presenter explains the Ralph loop, a bash while-loop that feeds an agent the same prompt over and over so each iteration starts with a fresh, small context window. He splits the context window into zones: roughly the first 30% is the smart zone, 30 to 60% still performs well, and past about 60% quality degrades, with the exact numbers varying by model. Fixed overhead (system prompt, system tools, skills, MCP tools, the agent MD file) fills part of the smart zone before the user prompt, so he recommends keeping it small. The canonical loop works because the model cannot decide when to stop, and each task gets a clean window; he argues compaction is lossy because the model picks what to keep without knowing what matters. He criticises the official Claude Code Ralph plugin for compacting between iterations and for max-iteration and completion-promise limits. He flags Ryan Carson's variant, which appends to agents.md on every loop and adds tokens to every run. He praises Raz Mike's parallel-Ralph script, a browser-testing setup, and Matt Pocock's version that takes tasks from GitHub issues. The video ends with a sponsored pitch for Better Stack's MCP server that filters logs and frontend errors so the agent reads less. The evidence is the presenter's personal experience, with no benchmarks.
speakers: Better Stack presenter (not named in transcript)

key_ideas.idea: Context is split into zones: about 0 to 30% is the smart zone, 30 to 60% is still good, and beyond about 60% output quality degrades. The exact thresholds vary by model.
key_ideas.detail: The presenter uses a 200k-token window for Claude Sonnet or Opus as the example and calls the degradation zone the dumb zone. He admits the numbers are his own experience.

key_ideas.idea: The Ralph loop is a bash while-loop that gives the agent the same prompt on every pass. Each pass starts with a fresh context, so the agent always works in its smartest state.
key_ideas.detail: The canonical loop is credited to Jeff Huntley, who wrote about it in June of the previous year. The presenter calls the design genius because a new context is the default, not something the agent has to manage.

key_ideas.idea: Fixed overhead eats into the smart zone before any user prompt. System prompt, system tools, skills, MCP tools and the agent MD file are all loaded first.
key_ideas.detail: He cites roughly 8.3% of the context for the system prompt and 1.4% for system tools for a typical Claude model. Bigger agent MD files and more tools or skills push the start point further up, so he recommends keeping them lean.

key_ideas.idea: Use one goal per context window. The prompt inspects a plan file, picks the most important open task, implements it, runs tests, commits and pushes, then ticks the task off.
key_ideas.detail: The plan file is a high-level list such as build the frontend, build the backend, set up the database. He says a real setup should be more granular.

key_ideas.idea: The loop is controlled from outside the model. The model cannot stop it, so the operator can interrupt, edit the prompt file and restart whenever the agent drifts.
key_ideas.detail: He describes watching the loop as being a human on the loop, which reveals model-specific patterns that can be fixed in the prompt. He also says he would not cap iterations, because the loop sometimes finds useful fixes or features beyond the plan.

key_ideas.idea: Compaction is lossy and works against the loop. The official Claude Code Ralph plugin compacts earlier work into the next task instead of resetting the context, and it adds max-iteration and completion-promise limits.
key_ideas.detail: He says the model compacts by picking what it thinks matters, without knowing what the project needs, so critical information can be lost.

key_ideas.idea: Variants change the canonical loop in useful and harmful ways. Ryan Carson's version edits agents.md on each loop, which adds tokens to every run. Raz Mike's script runs parallel Ralphs. Matt Pocock's version reads tasks from GitHub issues.
key_ideas.detail: He says a team can reasonably tweak the loop for its own needs, but growing agents.md each iteration pushes the model toward the dumb zone.

key_ideas.idea: The closing sponsored segment argues that when many Ralphs produce software, errors need to be found and fixed. Better Stack's MCP server reads logs and frontend errors so the agent pulls only errors instead of whole logs.
key_ideas.detail: The argument is that filtering keeps the context small. The segment has no data on this effect.

techniques.name: Fresh-context bash Ralph loop
techniques.how: Write the task prompt to a prompt MD file. Run a bash while-loop that pipes the file into a new Claude Code invocation on each pass, using the skip-permissions flag (he shortens it on screen). Each iteration is a new process with a fresh context, and the loop, not the model, decides when to stop. Stop with Ctrl-C, edit the prompt file and restart.
techniques.when: Long, multi-task builds where each task should get the full smart zone and no compaction carries over between tasks.

techniques.name: Plan-file task selection
techniques.how: Keep a plan MD file with tasks. The prompt tells the agent to: read the plan, pick the most important unfinished task, implement it, run tests, commit and push, mark the task done in the plan, then stop. The loop repeats the same prompt.
techniques.when: When tasks are decomposed up front and each one can be verified by tests.

techniques.name: Keep fixed context small
techniques.how: Limit the number of MCP tools, skills and the size of the agent MD file, since all are loaded before the first user prompt. Check how much of the window the fixed overhead uses before adding more.
techniques.when: Before any long agent run, to keep more of the window in the smart zone.

techniques.name: Human-on-the-loop review
techniques.how: Watch the loop iterations instead of running them unattended, note recurring model mistakes, and add the corrections to the prompt file.
techniques.when: Early in a new loop or prompt, and when the agent starts going off the rails.

techniques.name: GitHub-issues task queue
techniques.how: Store each task as a GitHub issue. The loop picks the most important open issue, works it, closes it, then moves to the next. This is Matt Pocock's variant as described by the presenter.
techniques.when: When tasks already live in an issue tracker and you want the queue to be visible to humans.

techniques.name: Filter error output with an MCP server
techniques.how: Give the agent an MCP tool that returns only errors from logs or the frontend, instead of raw log files, so the context holds less noise.
techniques.when: When an agent debugs against large logs and the raw output would fill the window.

tools: Claude Code Ralph Wiggum plugin (Anthropic, slash command with max iterations and completion promise)
agent-browser tool (named Vasell in the captions)
Better Stack MCP server (log and frontend error search)
GPT-5 tokenizer (used for a token-count comparison)

numbers.claim: Typical Claude Sonnet or Opus context window is 200,000 tokens. The smart zone is about the first 60k tokens (30%), with degradation starting at about 60%.
System prompt takes about 8.3% of the context and system tools about 1.4% before the user prompt, per the presenter's Claude example.
60k tokens is roughly the full script of Star Wars: A New Hope, about 54,000 tokens with GPT-5's tokenizer.

hot_takes: Compaction loses critical information, so a fresh context per task beats compacting between iterations.
The official Claude Code Ralph plugin is wrong to use max-iteration caps and completion promises, since the loop should keep going and find things the plan missed.
Appending to agents.md on every loop adds tokens to every run and pushes the model into the dumb zone.
The zone thresholds are personal experience and vary by model. No benchmark is given.
The title says Anthropic messed up, but the video is mainly a comparison of community variants and a sponsor pitch.

relevance.why: ProsHarness wraps Claude Code and handles checkpoint and resume of long runs, loops and schedules. The video gives the canonical design: an external loop, one task per fresh context, and no compaction between tasks.
relevance.action: Compare ProsHarness loop iterations against a fresh-process-per-task design. Check whether checkpoint state can replace compaction between tasks, and make the stop condition harness-owned, not model-owned.

relevance.why: AgentOS measures token budgets and runs agent traffic through a proxy. The fixed-overhead point (system prompt, tools, skills, MCP tools) is measurable at that layer.
relevance.action: Log the fixed prompt overhead (system prompt, tool schemas, skills) per agent at the proxy, as a share of the context window, before the first user turn.
